message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it looks different depending on a few factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) and reflects shorter wavelengths (blue, green). So very deep ocean appears a deep blue or even indigo. |
| **Sunlight angle** | At noon, the sun is high and the water can look bright turquoise or greenish‑blue. In the early morning or late afternoon, the light is more oblique, giving a deeper, richer blue. |
| **Water clarity** | Clear water reflects more of the sky, so it can look sky‑blue. Turbid or algae‑rich water scatters light differently, often giving a green or brownish tint. |
| **Surface conditions** | Calm water reflects the sky more directly, while waves scatter light and can make the surface appear white or frothy. |
| **Location** | Coastal waters near reefs or kelp forests often look green or turquoise because of the vegetation and shallow depth. Open ocean far from land tends to be a deeper blue. |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” its actual hue can range from pale turquoise to deep indigo, sometimes with green or even brownish undertones depending on the conditions.
